Q001616:
Why this is correct:
Data Firehose streams flow logs to the SIEM in near real time, and S3 with Athena provides low-cost long-term retention and querying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch Logs for both: costly retention and not a streaming pipeline to the SIEM.
• Config: configuration, not flow logs.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: stream to SIEM + archive in S3.
Q001638:
Why this is correct:
Separate TGW route tables let PCI attachments learn only shared-services routes, so PCI VPCs have no route to non-PCI VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable propagation without separation: doesn't isolate.
• Separate TGW copying SGs: SGs don't control TGW routing.
• One table with blocking: fragile.

Key takeaway: segmentation on TGW = route table association/propagation.
Q001661:
Why this is correct:
An NLB-backed endpoint service lets consumer VPCs create interface endpoints, exposing only the service privately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway endpoint for an NLB: gateway endpoints are only for S3 and DynamoDB.
• Public ALB: internet exposure.
• Peering with every consumer: exposes networks.

Key takeaway: private SaaS exposure → PrivateLink.
Q001713:
Why this is correct:
Network Access Analyzer evaluates network paths against defined access scopes (for example, internet to sensitive subnets) across VPCs to find unintended access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Conformance packs: no path analysis.
• Reachability Analyzer per pair: not scalable.
• Network Monitor: performance probes.

Key takeaway: find unintended network paths → Network Access Analyzer.
Q001719:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route that traffic privately, bypassing NAT processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT instance: still in the path.
• More EIPs: no cost reduction.
• Interface endpoints cheaper than gateway: gateway endpoints are free.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB → gateway endpoints.
Q001730:
Why this is correct:
A stateless pass action forwards packets without state tracking, so return traffic isn't recognized as part of the flow. Forward traffic to the stateful engine (aws:forward_to_sfe) so return traffic is handled.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless can't match 443: it can.
• Missing route: not indicated.
• NAT for TLS: not required.

Key takeaway: use stateful inspection for bidirectional flows.
Q001765:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation renews automatically as long as the validation CNAME stays in DNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical renewal: email needs action.
• HTTP validation for ALB: not the ACM method here.
• Email renews without action: it needs approval.

Key takeaway: auto-renewing ACM → DNS validation.
Q001772:
Why this is correct:
A metric filter only sees events in its log group. If the trail doesn't deliver to that log group, the filter never matches.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default value 0: doesn't prevent matches.
• GuardDuty prerequisite: unrelated.
• Invalid JSON path: possible, but the delivery gap is the likely cause here.

Key takeaway: metric filters need the trail to deliver to that log group.
Q001773:
Why this is correct:
Enable Security Hub in each Region and use cross-Region aggregation into one Region for a single dashboard.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual review: tedious.
• Custom forwarders: unnecessary.
• S3 export with QuickSight: custom build.

Key takeaway: multi-Region findings → cross-Region aggregation.
Q001775:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule with a numeric filter on detail.severity (≥ 7) routes only high-severity findings to the Slack target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty can't be limited: no such setting.
• Metric filter on console logs: not a thing.
• Security Hub default notifications: not built-in filtering to Slack.

Key takeaway: route by severity with EventBridge filters.
Q001776:
Why this is correct:
A central event bus with a resource policy allowing the organization to PutEvents, plus forwarding rules in each account, centralizes findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local buckets polled hourly: slow.
• Assume roles to push: complex.
• Security Hub aggregation only: covers Security Hub, not every source here.

Key takeaway: cross-account events → central bus + org policy.
Q001777:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 scans the instance's EBS volumes when suspicious activity is detected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Protection: S3 access.
• Inspector reachability: network exposure.
• RDS Protection: database logins.

Key takeaway: scan for malware on EC2 → Malware Protection for EC2.
Q001778:
Why this is correct:
Without a normalized, aggregated view, analysts must correlate findings across separate consoles, which is slower and misses cross-service patterns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No findings without Security Hub: services generate findings independently.
• Consoles lack IAM: false.
• 24-hour history: false.

Key takeaway: aggregation speeds triage.
Q001779:
Why this is correct:
A metric published only when findings occur has no data otherwise. Treating missing data as notBreaching keeps the alarm OK between findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Change the unit: unrelated.
• Delete the alarm: loses alerting.
• Raise threshold: may miss single high findings.

Key takeaway: sparse metrics → set missing data behavior.
Q001780:
Why this is correct:
A composite alarm with AND logic pages once when both alarms are in ALARM together, reducing duplicate pages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Merged query: not an alarm.
• Anomaly bands: don't combine alarms.
• Shorter periods: more noise.

Key takeaway: reduce correlated pages → composite alarms.
Q001782:
Why this is correct:
Advanced event selectors can limit S3 data events to the five regulated buckets, controlling cost while keeping forensic detail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No data events: loses object-level visibility.
• All buckets: high cost.
• One Region: incomplete.

Key takeaway: scope data events with advanced selectors.
Q001783:
Why this is correct:
Return traffic to an ephemeral port was rejected. Security groups are stateful and allow it, so the likely cause is a NACL. Flow logs don't say which layer rejected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG stateless: false.
• Never REJECT when SG allows: NACL can reject.
• Shield blocked it: not how flow logs show it.

Key takeaway: REJECT on return traffic → suspect NACLs.
Q001784:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs don't capture traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS resolver. Use Route 53 Resolver query logging for DNS visibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS traffic filter: not an option.
• UDP missed: not the reason.
• S3-only: false.

Key takeaway: DNS visibility → Resolver query logs.
Q001785:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail S3 data events record the full userIdentity, session context, and MFA status for PutObject.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: IPs only.
• Server access logs: less identity detail.
• Config: configuration, not object writes.

Key takeaway: who wrote an object → CloudTrail data events.
Q001786:
Why this is correct:
A recurring (scheduled) Macie classification job scoped by the Classification=Confidential tag rescans those buckets, including new or changed objects.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty filter: not classification.
• One-time job: not periodic.
• Automated discovery: samples broadly, not a tag-scoped rescan.

Key takeaway: targeted periodic scans → scheduled Macie jobs.
Q001787:
Why this is correct:
Automated discovery samples objects across the account continuously, and classification jobs can be scheduled and scoped by bucket tags or names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 1 KB limit: false.
• Auto-remediates public buckets: Macie reports, doesn't fix.
• Encrypts objects: false.

Key takeaway: Macie = discovery and classification, not remediation.
Q001788:
Why this is correct:
The resource's Config timeline shows configuration changes over time and links to the CloudTrail events that made them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Proactive mode: pre-deployment checks.
• Conformance packs: rule bundles.
• Aggregators: multi-account views.

Key takeaway: what changed and who → Config timeline + CloudTrail.
Q001789:
Why this is correct:
A Config aggregator using the Organizations source collects compliance and configuration data from all member accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake federated queries: API activity.
• Rules in the central account: evaluate only that account.
• Security Hub native aggregation of Config data: not a replacement.

Key takeaway: multi-account Config view → aggregator.
Q001790:
Why this is correct:
Insights baselines normal management activity and flags significant deviations, and Insights events are delivered to trail destinations and EventBridge.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Analyzes Flow Logs: no.
• Manual thresholds: no.
• Requires S3 data events: no.

Key takeaway: CloudTrail Insights = baseline + anomalies on management events.
Q001791:
Why this is correct:
The bucket policy must allow CloudTrail to check the ACL (GetBucketAcl) and write objects (PutObject). Without it, no logs arrive.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Invalid prefix: possible, but the common issue is the policy.
• Disabled KMS key: only if encryption with that key is configured.
• CLI trails can't use manual buckets: false.

Key takeaway: trail delivery needs a correct bucket policy.
Q001792:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail needs permission in the SNS topic policy to publish. If it was changed, notifications stop.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket encryption: unrelated to SNS.
• Multi-Region: unrelated.
• Insights: unrelated.

Key takeaway: check the topic policy for missing notifications.
Q001793:
Why this is correct:
A suppression rule matching the finding type and the scanner's instances archives these expected findings automatically, while keeping other findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable the finding type: loses real detections.
• Threat list: generates more findings.
• Trusted IP list: applies to specific finding types and whole IPs.

Key takeaway: known benign activity → narrow suppression rules.
Q001794:
Why this is correct:
Trusted IP lists stop findings for traffic from listed IPs (for certain finding types), while threat lists generate findings for activity involving listed IPs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only in Security Hub: they're GuardDuty features.
• Threat lists not customizable: they are.
• Interchangeable: opposite effects.

Key takeaway: trusted = suppress; threat = alert.
Q001795:
Why this is correct:
An overly broad suppression rule hid more than intended. Narrow it to the finding type and specific resources, and review archived findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't cause this: suppression can.
• Deleted permanently: archived, not deleted.
• Only older findings: false.

Key takeaway: keep suppression rules narrow.
Q001796:
Why this is correct:
Organization trails are managed only from the management account or a delegated administrator. Member accounts can't stop or change them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP allow required: no.
• Daily quota: no.
• AdministratorAccess lacks StopLogging: it has it; the org trail is protected.

Key takeaway: org trails are centrally controlled.
Q001797:
Why this is correct:
A partitioned Athena table needs partitions added for new dates, or partition projection to compute them automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 30-day limit: false.
• Unsupported codec: false.
• Versioning: unrelated.

Key takeaway: new data not showing → partitions.
Q001798:
Why this is correct:
Athena reads columns by position, so the table DDL must match the custom format's field order.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parquet conversion: not required.
• Crawler fixes regardless: not reliable for custom order.
• Can't query custom formats: they can.

Key takeaway: custom log formats need matching DDL.
Q001799:
Why this is correct:
aws cloudtrail validate-logs checks the digest chain to prove whether log files were modified or deleted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual ETag comparison: not reliable.
• Insights events: unrelated.
• GuardDuty retroactive validation: no.

Key takeaway: prove log integrity → validate-logs.
Q001800:
Why this is correct:
Isolate with a quarantine security group, snapshot the EBS volumes for evidence, then investigate before remediating.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terminate immediately: destroys evidence.
• Delete volumes: destroys evidence.
• Account-wide SCP deny: disrupts everything.

Key takeaway: contain, preserve, then investigate.
Q001802:
Why this is correct:
Detective shows historical network connections, API call volumes, and role usage over time for the instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CVE reports: Inspector.
• Automatic quarantine: not Detective.
• Real-time blocking: not Detective.

Key takeaway: investigation context → Detective.
Q001804:
Why this is correct:
If snapshots weren't shared to the forensics account, a cross-account role or the KMS key policy for encrypted snapshots was likely missing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Severity threshold: would stop the whole workflow.
• Flow logs: unrelated to snapshot sharing.
• SSM Agent: relevant for memory capture, not snapshot sharing.

Key takeaway: cross-account evidence needs role and key permissions.
Q001805:
Why this is correct:
A tabletop exercise walks cross-functional participants through decisions and escalations to find gaps in the plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prefilled reports: not an exercise.
• Full permission lists: not the goal.
• Rebuild templates: not a tabletop.

Key takeaway: tabletop = people and decisions.
Q001806:
Why this is correct:
A targeted deny on the compromised principal, including revoking sessions issued before a time (aws:TokenIssueTime), contains the incident without disrupting everyone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Account-wide SCPs off-peak: still disruptive.
• Disable CloudTrail: destroys evidence.
• Delete the bucket: destroys evidence and data.

Key takeaway: contain narrowly.
Q001807:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds event management, DDoS cost protection, and Shield Response Team support, which strengthens a DDoS response playbook.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces the plan: no.
• Rebuilds instances: no.
• No WAF needed: WAF is still used for L7.

Key takeaway: Shield Advanced complements, not replaces, IR plans.
Q001808:
Why this is correct:
Detective builds behavior graphs from data ingested after an account joins, so recently added accounts have little history.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Needs Macie: no.
• Prior findings required: no.
• No S3 support: not the reason.

Key takeaway: Detective history starts when data ingestion starts.
Q001809:
Why this is correct:
The Automated Forensics Orchestrator for EC2, triggered through EventBridge and Step Functions, repeatably isolates and captures evidence.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual SSM: not automated.
• Config remediation: not forensics.
• Inspector remediation: not forensics.

Key takeaway: repeatable forensics → the orchestrator solution.
Q001811:
Why this is correct:
Standing privileged access speeds response but permanently increases attack surface. Just-in-time access reduces exposure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More auditable: not inherently.
• Identity Center can't grant temporary: it can.
• Removes MFA need: no.

Key takeaway: prefer just-in-time privileged access.
Q001812:
Why this is correct:
A spike in CreateAccessKey from an instance role suggests stolen credentials used for persistence. Revoke sessions, remove created keys, and review activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Benign drift: unlikely.
• Read-only role: then it wouldn't succeed.
• False positive: Detective correlates IAM events.

Key takeaway: unusual key creation = persistence attempt.
Q001813:
Why this is correct:
Runbooks should list current account IDs, role ARNs, and names so responders can act immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove forensics account: weakens response.
• Permanent admin: risky.
• Search docs live: slow.

Key takeaway: specific runbooks speed response.
Q001814:
Why this is correct:
Deactivate the exposed key immediately, then revoke sessions created with it (for example, with an inline deny based on aws:TokenIssueTime), then investigate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config tracking: doesn't stop access.
• Delete the user: loses evidence and may not end existing sessions.
• Rotate root: unrelated.

Key takeaway: exposed key → deactivate and revoke sessions.
Q001815:
Why this is correct:
Deactivating the key doesn't invalidate STS sessions already issued. Deny actions for tokens issued before a time (aws:TokenIssueTime).

Why the other options are wrong:
• False positives: sessions still work.
• GuardDuty lag: not the main reason.
• 24-hour delay: false.

Key takeaway: revoke existing temporary credentials explicitly.
Q001816:
Why this is correct:
Removing the instance profile doesn't revoke credentials already cached on the instance. A deny policy based on token issue time revokes them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: they differ.
• Only way: role session revocation is one of several steps.
• Removal invalidates cached creds: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: revoke role sessions, don't just detach profiles.
Q001817:
Why this is correct:
An isolation security group cuts communication while keeping the instance running for memory and disk forensics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terminate: loses evidence.
• Stop: loses memory.
• Black-hole route: affects the whole subnet.

Key takeaway: isolate but preserve.
Q001818:
Why this is correct:
Security groups apply per ENI. If the instance has multiple ENIs, each needs the isolation group.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable the profile: not network isolation.
• Nothing further: other ENIs remain open.
• Restart: unnecessary and loses memory.

Key takeaway: isolate every network interface.
Q001820:
Why this is correct:
Enable Block Public Access, fix the bucket policy, and preserve evidence (for example, object versions and logs, with legal hold if needed).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the bucket: destroys evidence and data.
• Encryption: doesn't revoke public access.
• Rotate access keys: buckets don't have keys.

Key takeaway: close exposure and preserve evidence.
Q001821:
Why this is correct:
Account-level Block Public Access contains exposure quickly across all buckets but may break legitimate public uses. A targeted deny policy is narrower but slower.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Account level unsupported: it is.
• Deny evaluated after BPA: not the point.
• Only new buckets: applies to all.

Key takeaway: broad BPA vs. targeted policy is a blast-radius tradeoff.
Q001822:
Why this is correct:
Block Public Access affects anonymous and public access. Unexpired pre-signed URLs from permitted principals still work until they expire or the signer's credentials are revoked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stale CloudTrail: no.
• 24-hour propagation: no.
• Same-account role unaffected: not the case described.

Key takeaway: revoke signer credentials to kill pre-signed URLs.
Q001823:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge routes Security Hub findings to a Step Functions workflow that remediates, notifies via SNS, and opens a ticket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email only: manual.
• Config auto-remediation only: not the full workflow.
• Manual console review: slow.

Key takeaway: orchestrated remediation → EventBridge + Step Functions.
Q001824:
Why this is correct:
Fully automated remediation risks disruptive actions on false positives. Add human approval for destructive steps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One Lambda per execution: false.
• GuardDuty not in EventBridge: false.
• Not logged: Step Functions and CloudTrail log it.

Key takeaway: gate destructive automation.
Q001825:
Why this is correct:
Effective permissions are limited by the permissions boundary. Adding iam:PutRolePolicy to the boundary lets the function attach the deny policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the boundary: weakens guardrails.
• Boundaries only for users: they apply to roles.
• AdministratorAccess: still limited by the boundary.

Key takeaway: boundaries cap permissions; update the boundary.
Q001826:
Why this is correct:
Reset the root password, remove any root access keys, confirm MFA, and review CloudTrail for root activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete root: not possible.
• SCP only: doesn't cover the management account and isn't enough.
• Identity Center locks root: no.

Key takeaway: root compromise → reset, remove keys, MFA, investigate.
Q001827:
Why this is correct:
A security group allowing only HTTPS egress to SSM endpoints (for example, via VPC endpoints) keeps Session Manager and Run Command working while isolating the instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all rules: SSM stops working.
• Detach profile: SSM needs the role.
• Disable the ENI: loses access.

Key takeaway: isolate while keeping management access.
Q001828:
Why this is correct:
Overriding only the offending rule's action to Count stops false positives while keeping the rest of the managed rule group active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the whole group: loses protection.
• Shield Advanced: not a WAF rule fix.
• Change scope: not how it works.

Key takeaway: false positives → override one rule.
Q001830:
Why this is correct:
With OAC and SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must allow CloudFront's service principal to decrypt, scoped with aws:SourceArn to the distribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Re-enable OAI: OAC supports SSE-KMS.
• Disable encryption: weakens security.
• Viewer certificate permissions: unrelated.

Key takeaway: OAC + SSE-KMS → key policy for CloudFront.
Q001831:
Why this is correct:
A stateful rule group with domain-list rules inspects the TLS SNI (and HTTP host) to allow or block outbound domains.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless IP rules: domains change IPs.
• Flow logs dropping flows: not possible.
• CloudFront WAF: inbound web traffic.

Key takeaway: egress domain filtering → Network Firewall domain lists.
Q001833:
Why this is correct:
DDoS cost protection applies to charges caused by a DDoS on a Shield Advanced-protected resource. Request credits through Support.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enterprise Support and BAA: not required.
• Health checks disabled: unrelated.
• DRT pre-approval: not required.

Key takeaway: cost protection only for protected resources.
Q001834:
Why this is correct:
A CloudFront Function on viewer response adds security headers at the edge cheaply and with minimal latency for every response. (Response headers policies are another built-in option.)

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda@Edge origin request: wrong event and more cost.
• API Gateway authorizer: unrelated.
• WAF block response: not for adding headers.

Key takeaway: lightweight header changes → CloudFront Functions or response headers policies.
Q001835:
Why this is correct:
Rotating IPs evade IP-only rate limits. A custom aggregate key combining source IP with the attempted-account header (or just the account header) rate-limits attempts per target account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer window with IP only: rotating IPs still evade.
• Geo block: attackers are global or local.
• CAPTCHA without aggregation change: still keyed on IP.
• Disable the rule: L3/L4 mitigation doesn't stop credential stuffing.

Key takeaway: match the aggregation key to the attack pattern.
Q001836:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment keeps both directions of each flow in the same AZ, so stateful firewalls see complete sessions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single AZ: loses resilience.
• Stateless rules: lose stateful inspection.
• More capacity units: doesn't fix asymmetry.

Key takeaway: TGW + stateful inspection → appliance mode.
Q001837:
Why this is correct:
With OAC, the bucket policy must allow the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal (with an AWS:SourceArn condition for the distribution), not the old OAI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning incompatible: no.
• No HTTPS with OAC: false.
• Public bucket needed: no.

Key takeaway: migrating to OAC → update the bucket policy.
Q001839:
Why this is correct:
Containers behind a bridge add a network hop, so IMDSv2 responses with hop limit 1 don't reach them. Raise the hop limit to 2 where containers need IMDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG rule to 169.254.169.254: SGs don't govern IMDS.
• Containers can't use IMDSv2: they can.
• Token TTL: unrelated to hops.

Key takeaway: containers + IMDSv2 → hop limit 2.
Q001840:
Why this is correct:
Using awsvpc mode with ECS_AWSVPC_BLOCK_IMDS (or iptables rules) blocks tasks from reaching the instance role via IMDS, so each task uses only its task role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same broad role everywhere: no least privilege.
• SG outbound deny to IMDS: SGs can't block it.
• IMDSv2 hop limit 1 in bridge mode: blocks IMDS but the option's claim is overstated.

Key takeaway: stop tasks from borrowing the instance role.
Q001841:
Why this is correct:
ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector) continuously scans OS and programming language packages and rescans when new CVEs appear.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty Malware for ECR: not CVE scanning.
• Config conformance packs: configuration.
• Basic scanning: OS packages at push only.

Key takeaway: continuous image CVE scanning → enhanced scanning.
Q001842:
Why this is correct:
A custom patch baseline with severity-based auto-approval, patch groups, and maintenance windows installs critical patches within the required time, with compliance reporting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config installing patches: not its role.
• Default baseline can't be customized: you create custom ones.
• Monthly SSH: slow and manual.

Key takeaway: patch SLAs → custom baselines + windows.
Q001844:
Why this is correct:
If the web app was abused (for example, via SSRF) to read role credentials from IMDS, requiring IMDSv2 on launch templates and running instances blocks that path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rotate root: unrelated.
• Block Public Access: unrelated.
• Long-term keys: worse.
• Deny all inbound: breaks the site.

Key takeaway: SSRF credential theft → IMDSv2.
Q001845:
Why this is correct:
IRSA gives each pod's service account its own role, achieving pod-level least privilege at the cost of more roles to manage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fargate only: works on EC2 nodes too.
• Requires privileged pods: no.
• No roles needed: it uses roles.

Key takeaway: pod-level IAM → IRSA.
Q001847:
Why this is correct:
Inspector's Lambda code scanning is a separate feature that must be enabled and supports specific runtimes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Needs AdministratorAccess: no.
• Must be invoked: not required.
• Can't scan Lambda: it can.

Key takeaway: enable each Inspector scan type.
Q001848:
Why this is correct:
Basic scanning checks OS packages at push time. Enhanced scanning (Inspector) covers OS and language packages and rescans continuously.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed coverage: incorrect.
• Identical: they differ.
• Enhanced one-time: it's continuous.

Key takeaway: enhanced = broader and continuous.
Q001849:
Why this is correct:
If the workload doesn't use IMDS at all, disabling the metadata endpoint (HttpEndpoint=disabled) removes the attack surface entirely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IMDSv2 is maximum: disabling is stronger when IMDS isn't needed.
• Hop limit 0: invalid.
• SG rule to IMDS: SGs can't block it.

Key takeaway: not needed → disable IMDS.
Q001851:
Why this is correct:
Responses come back to ephemeral ports. A stateless NACL must allow inbound ephemeral ports from the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT route missing: requests succeed, so outbound works.
• NACLs can't be used: they can.
• Inbound 443 on SG: return traffic is stateful.

Key takeaway: NACLs need rules for return traffic.
Q001852:
Why this is correct:
A gateway endpoint policy scoped to the approved bucket limits what the VPC can reach, and a bucket policy with aws:sourceVpce limits the bucket to that endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NACL S3 IP denies: impractical.
• IAM alone: endpoint policies can restrict buckets.
• NAT instead: loses the private path.

Key takeaway: two-way lock-down: endpoint policy + bucket policy.
Q001853:
Why this is correct:
For requests to resolve to the interface endpoint, private DNS must be enabled on the endpoint and the VPC's enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames must be on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete NAT first: not required.
• No private DNS for DynamoDB interface endpoints: private DNS options exist.
• Only new resources: not true.

Key takeaway: interface endpoints rely on private DNS.
Q001854:
Why this is correct:
Security groups can't deny traffic. A NACL deny rule (with a low rule number) blocks the IP for the subnet immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deny in SGs: not possible.
• WAF: only for web traffic through supported resources.
• SGs support deny: false.

Key takeaway: block an IP at the subnet → NACL deny.
Q001855:
Why this is correct:
A single shared route table with full propagation lets every VPC reach every other. Give PCI attachments their own route table with only approved routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permissive SG: not the segmentation failure.
• TGW can't segment: it can.
• Appliance mode: symmetry, not segmentation.
• Disable propagation account-wide: disruptive.

Key takeaway: segmentation needs separate route tables.
Q001856:
Why this is correct:
Interface endpoints keep traffic to the AWS API off the public internet, at the cost of per-AZ hourly and data processing fees.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No security gain: removes internet exposure.
• No API charges: false.
• Must drop Direct Connect: false.

Key takeaway: private API access costs per endpoint.
Q001857:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center with an external IdP and permission sets provides single sign-on to all 40 accounts with centrally managed access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• IAM users + switch role: long-term credentials.
• AD with RDP bastions: not AWS access.

Key takeaway: multi-account SSO → Identity Center.
Q001858:
Why this is correct:
The permission set must be provisioned to the account (which creates the role) before users see access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IdP sync delay: possible but not the stated cause.
• Delegated admin: not required.
• Users only: groups are supported.

Key takeaway: assign and provision permission sets.
Q001859:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center creates and updates roles from permission sets in all assigned accounts, centralizing management. Per-account SAML providers require maintaining roles in each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-account SAML unsupported: supported.
• No roles needed: it creates roles.
• Only method for temporary credentials: SAML also gives temporary credentials.

Key takeaway: central permission management → Identity Center.
Q001861:
Why this is correct:
ABAC only works if policies compare aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter with resource tags. Check the policy conditions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MFA: unrelated.
• Config rules: unrelated.
• Management account: unrelated.

Key takeaway: ABAC requires tag-comparing policies.
Q001862:
Why this is correct:
A user pool handles sign-up and sign-in (with MFA), and an identity pool exchanges tokens for scoped temporary AWS credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity pool unauthenticated only: no sign-in.
• User pool ID token as AWS credentials: it isn't.
• Identity Center: workforce, not customers.

Key takeaway: app users + AWS access → user pool + identity pool.
Q001863:
Why this is correct:
GetCredentialsForIdentity fails if the IAM role's trust policy doesn't trust cognito-identity.amazonaws.com with the right conditions, or if role mapping is misconfigured.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Client secret: user pool concern.
• CloudFront: unrelated.
• Same account as bucket: not required.

Key takeaway: identity pool issues → role trust and mappings.
Q001865:
Why this is correct:
A Pre Token Generation trigger can add a trusted TenantID claim, mapped to a principal tag for IAM conditions, so users can't set it themselves.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoded roles per tenant: scaling issues.
• Client-supplied header: untrusted.
• User-set custom attribute: users could change it.

Key takeaway: tenant isolation needs trusted claims.
Q001866:
Why this is correct:
Create a SAML identity provider in IAM from the AD FS metadata, a role that trusts it, and configure AD FS to send Role and RoleSessionName claims.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OIDC provider for AD FS: SAML is the fit here.
• IAM user per employee: not federation.
• AD FS calling CreateUser: not federation.

Key takeaway: SAML federation = provider + trusting role + claims.
Q001867:
Why this is correct:
SAML assertions have validity windows. Clock skew on the IdP server makes assertions appear expired or not yet valid.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MFA not enforced: different error.
• Session duration too high: different error.
• Wrong Region: IAM is global.

Key takeaway: intermittent SAML validity errors → check clocks.
Q001868:
Why this is correct:
Registering GitHub's OIDC provider and scoping the role trust with sub and aud conditions lets workflows get temporary credentials without stored keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stored access keys: long-term.
• Root keys: never.
• IAM user password: not for API access.

Key takeaway: CI without keys → OIDC federation.
Q001869:
Why this is correct:
For workloads with an OIDC issuer (such as a Kubernetes cluster), register the issuer and use AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both need Identity Center: no.
• OIDC not for workloads: it's common for them.
• OIDC only for Cognito: false.

Key takeaway: workload identity → OIDC.
Q001870:
Why this is correct:
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity fails if the trust policy's conditions don't match the token's aud and sub claims.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access key instead of token: not this flow.
• Missing permissions policy: affects later calls, not assuming the role.
• Different partition: unlikely.

Key takeaway: OIDC trust conditions must match token claims.
Q001871:
Why this is correct:
Deny all actions when MFA is absent, except the self-service actions needed to set up MFA (such as iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice and EnableMFADevice).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root settings inherited: no.
• Deny everything without exceptions: users can't set up MFA.
• SCP denying iam:*: too broad.

Key takeaway: MFA enforcement needs a bootstrap exception.
Q001872:
Why this is correct:
SCPs apply uniformly across the OU but never grant permissions. Identity policies can be edited by account admins and apply per principal.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs grant permissions: they don't.
• Condition not in SCPs: SCPs support conditions.
• Identity policies org-wide: they're per principal.

Key takeaway: SCP = uniform ceiling; identity policy = per-principal.
Q001874:
Why this is correct:
A Deny on only sensitive actions with BoolIfExists aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false requires MFA where it matters without blocking read-only work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundary removed for read-only: fragile.
• Config reversal: after the fact.
• MFA for every call: disruptive.

Key takeaway: require MFA selectively for sensitive actions.
Q001876:
Why this is correct:
A permissions boundary limits effective permissions. If it doesn't include dynamodb:PutItem, the identity policy's allow has no effect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundaries only for roles: they apply to users and roles.
• Must duplicate exactly: it must include the action.
• DynamoDB unsupported: boundaries are IAM-wide.

Key takeaway: effective = identity ∩ boundary.
Q001877:
Why this is correct:
Requiring a specific permissions boundary on every role developers create keeps delegated roles within safe limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: unsafe.
• Roles don't support boundaries: they do.
• Config detection only: after the fact.

Key takeaway: delegated role creation → boundaries.
Q001878:
Why this is correct:
Besides the target's trust policy, the caller in Account A needs an identity policy allowing sts:AssumeRole on that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policy: unrelated.
• Organizations required: no.
• Must list user ARN: account ID trust works.

Key takeaway: AssumeRole needs trust and caller permission.
Q001879:
Why this is correct:
SCPs and permissions boundaries only limit permissions. Resource-based policies can grant access, including to other accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundaries at org level: they're per principal.
• Only resource policies deny: all can deny.
• Interchangeable: they differ.

Key takeaway: limits vs. grants.
Q001880:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy in Account A granting B's role access to the prefix, plus an identity policy in B allowing it, enables cross-account access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared IAM user keys: insecure.
• Public bucket: insecure.
• Bucket policy only: B's role also needs permission (cross-account).

Key takeaway: cross-account = both sides.
Q001881:
Why this is correct:
KMS requires the key policy to allow the principal or delegate to IAM policies (via the account root statement). Otherwise the IAM allow is ignored.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM ignored entirely: not if the key policy delegates.
• SCP allow needed: SCPs don't grant.
• No resource policies: key policies are resource policies.

Key takeaway: KMS access starts with the key policy.
Q001882:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying access when aws:PrincipalOrgID doesn't match the organization's ID blocks principals outside the org.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning: unrelated.
• Block Public Access only: doesn't stop authenticated outside accounts.
• External account policies: not under your control.

Key takeaway: org-only access → aws:PrincipalOrgID.
Q001883:
Why this is correct:
KMS grants give temporary, fine-grained permissions to a principal and can be created and retired via API without editing the key policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Edit key policy per request: fragile.
• SCP per request: inappropriate.
• Grants unsupported: they exist.

Key takeaway: temporary key access → KMS grants.
Q001886:
Why this is correct:
A few ABAC policies comparing principal and resource project tags scale to many tenants without per-project roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Role per project: explodes roles.
• ARNs in resource policies: unmanageable.
• One broad policy: no isolation.

Key takeaway: multi-tenant scale → ABAC.
Q001887:
Why this is correct:
Tag keys and values are case-sensitive in policy evaluation, so department and Department don't match.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ABAC only for EC2: false.
• ABAC ignores case: false.
• Recreate resource: not required.

Key takeaway: tag case must match exactly.
Q001888:
Why this is correct:
ABAC scales by tagging principals and resources, while RBAC needs new roles or policies per team or project.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RBAC fewer policies: not at scale.
• ABAC only with Identity Center: works with IAM roles too.
• ABAC can't use Deny: it can.

Key takeaway: ABAC scales with tags.
Q001889:
Why this is correct:
Sending a PrincipalTag SAML attribute makes STS apply it as a session tag, which policies can use for ABAC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No session tags from SAML: they're supported.
• S3 object tags: not session identity.
• Manual role tags: not per user.

Key takeaway: per-user attributes → session tags.
Q001891:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions externalizes app authorization into Cedar policies evaluated by IsAuthorized.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policies on documents: IAM isn't for app-level resources.
• GuardDuty: detection.
• WAF: request filtering, not authorization.

Key takeaway: app authorization → Verified Permissions.
Q001892:
Why this is correct:
IAM governs access to AWS APIs. Verified Permissions governs authorization decisions inside your application. They complement each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces IAM: no.
• S3 only: no.
• Mutually exclusive: no.

Key takeaway: AWS access vs. app access.
Q001893:
Why this is correct:
A Cedar policy specifies principal, action, and resource, with optional when and unless conditions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ARN and Region only: incomplete.
• Stack name and timestamp: unrelated.
• SG and route table: unrelated.

Key takeaway: Cedar = principal, action, resource, conditions.
Q001894:
Why this is correct:
An unexpected Deny often means the request's entity types or IDs don't match the schema or policy definitions. Check them first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Service malfunction: unlikely.
• SCPs: don't affect Verified Permissions decisions.
• Recreate the store: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: debug by checking entity types and IDs.
Q001895:
Why this is correct:
A TCP listener passes TLS through unchanged, so TLS terminates on the instances end to end.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS listener: terminates at the NLB.
• SSL policy forcing termination: terminates at the NLB.
• HTTPS listener: NLBs don't have HTTPS listeners.

Key takeaway: end-to-end TLS through NLB → TCP passthrough.
Q001896:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation needs the CNAME record in the zone that's authoritative for the domain, even if it's in another account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requests expire in 72 hours: they can remain pending longer.
• Cross-account impossible: just create the record there.
• Must request in the zone's account: no.

Key takeaway: create the validation CNAME wherever the zone lives.
Q001897:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront in front of both origins, with an ACM certificate in us-east-1, terminates TLS at edge locations near users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB in front of CloudFront: backwards.
• S3 website endpoint: no HTTPS.
• Regional ALBs with latency routing: no edge termination.

Key takeaway: global TLS latency → CloudFront.
Q001898:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates trusted only inside the organization, suited to service-to-service TLS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public ACM: for public names.
• Email validation: still public.
• Self-signed via S3: unmanaged trust.

Key takeaway: internal TLS → Private CA.
Q001899:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway mutual TLS on a custom domain, with a truststore in S3, verifies each client's certificate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resource policies by VPC endpoint: not client identity.
• Bearer tokens: not certificates.
• WAF can't inspect client certs: not how it works.

Key takeaway: client certificate auth → API Gateway mTLS.
Q001900:
Why this is correct:
ACM doesn't renew imported certificates. The imported certificate expired, causing handshake failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB not eligible: ACM-issued certificates renew on NLB.
• CloudFront only: false.
• Renewal quota: no.

Key takeaway: imported certs need manual renewal.
Q001901:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports mutual TLS in verify mode with a trust store in S3 holding the CA bundle.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Authorization header rules: not mTLS.
• TLS 1.3 policy: not client auth.
• CLB required: ALB supports mTLS.

Key takeaway: mTLS at the load balancer → ALB verify mode.
Q001903:
Why this is correct:
Tunnels that won't come up usually mean a mismatched pre-shared key or IKE phase 1/phase 2 parameters.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VGW EIP: not how VGWs work.
• Multiple route tables: unrelated.
• Static routing: doesn't stop tunnels establishing.

Key takeaway: tunnels down → check PSK and IKE settings.
Q001905:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region snapshot copies must be encrypted with a KMS key in the destination Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Source key policy for another Region: keys are Regional.
• Can't copy encrypted snapshots: they can.
• Decrypt first: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: cross-Region encrypted copies → destination-Region key.
Q001906:
Why this is correct:
Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents deletion or retention changes by anyone, including root, for 7 years.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Governance mode: privileged users can bypass.
• Lifecycle: moves data; doesn't lock it.
• MFA Delete: the owner can disable it.

Key takeaway: no one can delete → Compliance mode.
Q001907:
Why this is correct:
Glacier Vault Lock applies a vault lock policy that becomes immutable once locked, enforcing retention controls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lock on Deep Archive objects: applies to S3 buckets, not Glacier vaults.
• Vault access policy: can be changed.
• Permissions boundary: can be changed.

Key takeaway: immutable Glacier vault controls → Vault Lock.
Q001908:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides a single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSM cluster under the customer's control.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Secrets Manager: secrets storage.
• KMS AWS managed keys: shared service.
• KMS default key store: multi-tenant HSMs.

Key takeaway: single-tenant validated HSMs → CloudHSM.
Q001909:
Why this is correct:
A KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM lets apps keep using the KMS API while key material lives in the company's CloudHSM cluster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS owned key: no control.
• PKCS#11 everywhere: changes applications.
• Secrets Manager: not a key store.

Key takeaway: KMS API + your HSM → custom key store.
Q001910:
Why this is correct:
IAM administrator rights don't override KMS: the key policy must allow the principal directly or delegate to IAM policies (the account root statement).

Why the other options are wrong:
• MFA requirement: not inherent.
• IAM ignored entirely: not when delegated.
• Same OU: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: key policy first for KMS.
Q001911:
Why this is correct:
Existing unencrypted volumes can't be encrypted in place. Snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption, create a new volume, and swap it in.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EnableKeyRotation: unrelated.
• Encryption by default: only new volumes.
• modify-volume --encrypted: not supported.

Key takeaway: encrypt existing EBS via snapshot copy.
Q001912:
Why this is correct:
RDS encryption can't be enabled in place. Snapshot, copy with encryption and a KMS key, restore a new instance, and cut over.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Set StorageEncrypted: not allowed on existing instances.
• TDE retroactively: not the RDS mechanism.
• Support migration: not offered.

Key takeaway: encrypt existing RDS via encrypted snapshot copy.
Q001913:
Why this is correct:
KMS multi-Region keys share key material across Regions (primary plus replicas), fitting customer managed encryption for global tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed keys identical across Regions: they aren't.
• Grants across Regions: keys are Regional.
• Single-Region key cross-Region: not possible.

Key takeaway: cross-Region CMKs → multi-Region keys.
Q001914:
Why this is correct:
Alternating-users rotation switches between two database users, so the previous credential stays valid while the new one propagates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Emailing passwords: insecure.
• Disable rotation: fails the requirement.
• Single-user rotation: brief window where old credentials fail.

Key takeaway: zero-downtime rotation → alternating users.
Q001915:
Why this is correct:
The rotation function must run in a VPC that can reach both the RDS instance and the Secrets Manager endpoint (via VPC endpoint or NAT). Otherwise it times out.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS rotation: unrelated.
• GetRandomPassword permission: would cause AccessDenied.
• Can't rotate private DBs: they can.

Key takeaway: rotation Lambdas need network paths to both.
Q001917:
Why this is correct:
A Macie delegated administrator designated through Organizations manages jobs and findings for all member accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate per account: fragmented.
• Custom identifier via RAM: not how Macie is centralized.
• Config aggregators: not Macie.

Key takeaway: org-wide Macie → delegated administrator.
Q001918:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty detects threats such as compromised credentials. Macie discovers PII in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: incorrect.
• Config for both: not these functions.
• Identical: different services.

Key takeaway: threats → GuardDuty; sensitive data → Macie.
Q001919:
Why this is correct:
KMS Encrypt handles up to 4 KB. Envelope encryption generates a data key (GenerateDataKey), encrypts the file locally, and stores the encrypted data key with it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sign API: signing, not encryption.
• Quota increase: not possible.
• 4 KB chunks: slow and costly.

Key takeaway: large data → envelope encryption.
Q001920:
Why this is correct:
A KMS grant gives Account A temporary use of the key and can be retired after the migration, without editing the key policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent statement removed manually: error-prone.
• Temporary role: workable but grants are purpose-built.
• RAM sharing: KMS keys aren't shared via RAM.

Key takeaway: time-bound key access → grants.
Q001921:
Why this is correct:
A custom rotation Lambda implementing createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, and finishSecret can call the vendor's API to rotate the key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store rotation: none built in.
• Not possible: custom rotation exists.
• Config remediation: not rotation.

Key takeaway: non-database secrets → custom rotation Lambda.
Q001922:
Why this is correct:
Each secret can be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key you specify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always AWS managed: false.
• GovCloud only: false.
• Manual export and import: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: CMK for secrets → set KmsKeyId.
Q001923:
Why this is correct:
Scheduled jobs with sampling and criteria such as prefixes or last-modified dates reduce the volume scanned and cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable Macie: loses discovery.
• Custom identifiers are free: scanning still costs.
• Deep Archive to avoid scanning: evasive and impractical.

Key takeaway: control Macie cost with scoping and sampling.
Q001924:
Why this is correct:
Call GenerateDataKey once, cache the plaintext data key briefly in memory, and encrypt items locally, reducing KMS calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypt per item: many network calls.
• Store CMK material locally: not possible and unsafe.
• WithoutPlaintext: gives no plaintext key to encrypt now.

Key takeaway: many small items → reuse a data key.
Q001925:
Why this is correct:
An SCP denying all actions when aws:PrincipalArn is the root user blocks root usage in member accounts (SCPs don't apply to the management account).

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policy on accounts: can't attach to root.
• Boundary on root: not possible.
• Deny assuming OrganizationAccountAccessRole: different concern.

Key takeaway: restrict member root → SCP on root ARN.
Q001927:
Why this is correct:
Separate Sandbox and Production OUs let each have its own SCPs and guardrails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All under root with IAM: no guardrails.
• One OU with tags: weak separation.
• Sandbox under Production: inherits production restrictions.

Key takeaway: different environments → different OUs.
Q001928:
Why this is correct:
Designating a Security Tooling account as delegated administrator moves security service management out of the management account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable services: loses detection.
• Manage in each account: fragmented.
• Scoped roles in management account: still uses the management account.

Key takeaway: keep the management account minimal → delegated admin.
Q001929:
Why this is correct:
SCPs apply across the account and its ancestor OUs. If the deny isn't working, check each SCP in the path, including conditions and whether the deny is actually attached where expected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs only warn: they block.
• Can't use aws:RequestedRegion: they can.
• OR logic: denies win.

Key takeaway: trace the SCP inheritance path.
Q001930:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail automatically logs every current and future member account to the Log Archive bucket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-account trails: manual.
• Guardrails alone: don't create logging.
• Config aggregators: not CloudTrail logs.

Key takeaway: org-wide logging → organization trail.
Q001931:
Why this is correct:
SCPs cap permissions for every principal in the accounts they apply to. Permissions boundaries cap a single user or role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both grant: neither grants.
• Boundaries for root: no.
• Identical: different scope.

Key takeaway: SCP = account-wide ceiling; boundary = per principal.
Q001932:
Why this is correct:
If a guardrail seems not to apply, the account or OU may have drifted from the Control Tower baseline. Repair or re-register it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only new accounts: guardrails apply to enrolled accounts.
• Only new resources: preventive guardrails block actions.
• Never prevented: preventive guardrails exist.

Key takeaway: guardrail anomalies → check drift.
Q001933:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower guardrails are maintained by AWS but opinionated. Custom SCPs are flexible but require you to maintain them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't coexist: they can.
• Custom SCPs self-update: they don't.
• Custom SCPs never useful: they are for specific needs.

Key takeaway: managed controls vs. custom flexibility.
Q001934:
Why this is correct:
Sharing the VPC subnets through AWS RAM lets application accounts launch into them while networking keeps ownership.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs grant access: they don't.
• Account Factory copies: separate VPCs.
• Roles modifying the networking account: over-privileged.

Key takeaway: shared subnets → RAM.
Q001935:
Why this is correct:
AWS Signer signs deployment packages, and a Lambda code signing configuration rejects unsigned or untrusted code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default pipeline role: no integrity.
• Public bucket: insecure.
• Versioning: not integrity verification.

Key takeaway: trusted Lambda code → Signer + code signing config.
Q001936:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed permissions integrate with Organizations and auto-deploy stacks to new accounts in target OUs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed can't target OUs: self-managed doesn't auto-deploy.
• Self-managed extends automatically: false.
• Either: only service-managed auto-deploys.

Key takeaway: auto-deploy to new accounts → service-managed StackSets.
Q001937:
Why this is correct:
A launch constraint provisions the product with a specified IAM role, so developers don't need permissions to create RDS directly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Portfolio sharing: distribution only.
• TagOptions: tags.
• Stack policies: updates.

Key takeaway: least privilege self-service → launch constraints.
Q001938:
Why this is correct:
Running cfn-guard or cfn-nag in an early CodeBuild stage fails the pipeline on risky templates before deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security Hub after production: too late.
• Drift detection after deployment: too late.
• Deny CreateStack: blocks everything.

Key takeaway: shift-left template checks.
Q001939:
Why this is correct:
Self-managed StackSets need an execution role in each target account that trusts the administrator account's role. Without it, deployment fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Target must be management account: no.
• Syntax error shows as assume failure: no.
• Only management OU: no.

Key takeaway: self-managed StackSets need execution roles.
Q001940:
Why this is correct:
The cross-account role needs kms:Decrypt on the artifact bucket's KMS key via the key policy, plus S3 access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No cross-account support: it's supported.
• Disable versioning: unrelated.
• Public bucket: insecure.

Key takeaway: cross-account artifacts need key access.
Q001941:
Why this is correct:
TagOptions enforce allowed tag values on provisioned products, and portfolio sharing controls which accounts or OUs see the portfolio.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Notification/template constraints: not tagging.
• Service actions/StackSets: not the features.
• Launch constraints/stack policies: not tagging or visibility.

Key takeaway: Service Catalog tagging → TagOptions; visibility → sharing.
Q001942:
Why this is correct:
Scope iam:PassRole and CreateRole to specific roles with a required permissions boundary, and use a separate CloudFormation service role for deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all IAM permissions: may break builds.
• AdministratorAccess: worse.
• Disable CloudTrail: removes auditing.

Key takeaway: limit privilege escalation paths.
Q001943:
Why this is correct:
StackSets drift detection checks each stack instance for drift from the template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic deployment: provisioning, not drift.
• Conformance packs only way: no.
• Change sets: preview updates, not drift.

Key takeaway: StackSet compliance → drift detection.
Q001944:
Why this is correct:
For card payments, enable the PCI DSS standard plus AWS FSBP (and optionally CIS) in Security Hub.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CIS only: doesn't cover PCI.
• FSBP maps automatically to PCI: not fully.
• Duplicates Audit Manager: different purposes.

Key takeaway: match standards to regulations.
Q001945:
Why this is correct:
An organization conformance pack deployed from the delegated administrator applies the rule set to all accounts consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual per account: toil.
• Trusted Advisor: not Config rules.
• SCP replication: not how Config works.

Key takeaway: org-wide rule sets → conformance packs.
Q001946:
Why this is correct:
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization or account as the zone of trust finds resources shared with external principals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: limited checks.
• Macie: data classification.
• Config aggregators: no external access analysis.

Key takeaway: external access → Access Analyzer.
Q001948:
Why this is correct:
Findings from a Region reach the aggregation Region only if Security Hub is enabled there and the Region is linked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No cross-Region aggregation: it exists.
• GuardDuty can't forward: it can via Security Hub.
• Delegated admin only for itself: it manages members.

Key takeaway: cross-Region aggregation needs linked Regions.
Q001949:
Why this is correct:
Policy validation checks a policy for errors and best practices before use. External access findings show resources currently shared outside the zone of trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: incorrect.
• Validation only for identity policies: it covers resource policies too.
• Same feature: different.

Key takeaway: validation = before; findings = current exposure.
Q001950:
Why this is correct:
A single custom rule is simpler for one narrow requirement, while a conformance pack packages reusable rules for org-wide deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Packs need Security Hub: no.
• Identical deployment: they differ.
• Packs only managed rules: they can include custom rules.

Key takeaway: right-size the tool.
Q001951:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule filtering high-severity public-bucket findings invokes a remediation Lambda automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily CSV: slow and manual.
• Config remediation only: may not cover the finding source.
• CloudTrail Insights: API anomalies.

Key takeaway: auto-remediate specific findings → EventBridge filters.
Q001952:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager with a SOC 2 framework collects evidence from Config, Security Hub, and more, and maps it to controls for audits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raw exports equal evidence: auditors need mapping.
• Trusted Advisor: not SOC 2 evidence.
• Disable Config: loses evidence.

Key takeaway: audit-ready evidence → Audit Manager.
Q002053:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring watches process and network activity inside pods to detect mining and reverse shells.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Control plane audit logs: Kubernetes API calls, not processes.
• Inspector image scans: vulnerabilities before runtime.
• Manual flow log searches: slow and incomplete.

Key takeaway: runtime threats in containers → GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring.
Q002054:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail with log file validation, delivered to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode, centralizes logs, proves integrity, and prevents deletion.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Event history: 90 days, per account.
• MFA Delete: owners can disable it.
• Local per-account buckets: not central.

Key takeaway: central, tamper-evident, immutable logs.
Q002055:
Why this is correct:
Security Lake centralizes AWS and third-party security logs in OCSF format in your own data lake, with subscriber access for analytics tools.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security Hub insights: findings, not raw logs.
• Detective graphs: investigation, not a data lake.
• Logs Insights queries: not centralization.

Key takeaway: security data lake → Security Lake.
Q002056:
Why this is correct:
Swap in an isolation security group to cut C2 traffic, and snapshot the EBS volumes (and capture memory) to preserve evidence before further action.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terminate: destroys evidence.
• Reboot: loses memory evidence.
• Delete the finding: loses the record.

Key takeaway: contain and preserve before remediating.
Q002057:
Why this is correct:
Deactivate (then delete) the exposed key immediately, then review CloudTrail for any activity with it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Console password: not the exposed credential.
• Delete the repo: the key may already be copied.
• Enable MFA: doesn't block access keys.

Key takeaway: exposed key → deactivate first.
Q002058:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on high-severity GuardDuty EC2 findings starts a Step Functions workflow that tags, isolates, snapshots, and notifies consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily report: slow.
• Manual insights review: slow.
• SNS paging for manual steps: not automated.

Key takeaway: repeatable response → EventBridge + Step Functions.
Q002059:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR images, and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty Malware Protection: malware.
• Macie: sensitive data.
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.

Key takeaway: vulnerability management → Inspector.
Q002060:
Why this is correct:
Network Firewall with a stateful domain allow list (using SNI for HTTPS) permits only approved domains and blocks everything else.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SGs with domain names: not supported.
• NACL to 0.0.0.0/0: allows everything.
• NAT route limited to 443: can't filter domains.

Key takeaway: egress allow lists by domain → Network Firewall.
Q002061:
Why this is correct:
Requiring IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) with a low hop limit blocks SSRF from reading role credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS encryption: unrelated.
• Access keys in config: worse.
• Private subnet: SSRF still works from the app.

Key takeaway: SSRF protection → IMDSv2.
Q002062:
Why this is correct:
ABAC policies compare principal and resource project tags, so hundreds of projects need only a few policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resource policies with ARNs: unmanageable.
• Account per developer: excessive.
• Policy per project: sprawl.

Key takeaway: project-scoped access at scale → ABAC.
Q002063:
Why this is correct:
AdministratorAccess can still be denied by a permissions boundary that omits s3:DeleteBucket or by an SCP that denies it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trust policy: affects assuming, not calls afterward.
• Different Region: not an access denial cause.
• Block Public Access: unrelated to deleting buckets.

Key takeaway: effective permissions = policies ∩ boundaries ∩ SCPs.
Q002064:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions with Cedar policies handles attribute-based app authorization such as amount and department limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM per end user: not for app users.
• WAF rules: not authorization logic.
• Cognito groups only: too coarse.

Key takeaway: fine-grained app authorization → Verified Permissions.
Q002065:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center with SAML sign-in from the external IdP and SCIM provisioning gives single sign-on to all accounts with automatic user sync.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito for workforce: wrong tool.
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• Synced IAM users: long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: workforce SSO + sync → Identity Center with SCIM.
Q002066:
Why this is correct:
A KMS multi-Region key with a replica in us-west-2 lets data encrypted in us-east-1 be decrypted in us-west-2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Export key material: not possible from KMS.
• Separate keys with same alias: different material.
• SSE-S3: loses customer key control.

Key takeaway: cross-Region decryption → multi-Region keys.
Q002067:
Why this is correct:
Object Lock in compliance mode prevents overwriting or deletion by anyone, including root, for the retention period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning with expiry: allows deletion.
• Bucket policy deny: admins can change it.
• Governance mode: privileged users can bypass.

Key takeaway: regulatory immutability → compliance mode.
Q002068:
Why this is correct:
A KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM keeps keys in single-tenant HSMs the company controls, while services still use KMS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default key store: multi-tenant.
• SSE-S3: AWS-managed keys.
• Secrets Manager: not an HSM.

Key takeaway: single-tenant HSM keys with KMS integration → custom key store.
Q002069:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying all actions when aws:SecureTransport is false rejects any non-HTTPS request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• Server-side encryption condition: at rest.
• Default SSE-KMS: at rest.

Key takeaway: enforce TLS to S3 → SecureTransport deny.
Q002070:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks to block noncompliant resources before they're provisioned.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs only: can't inspect resource properties at creation for every case.
• Security Hub after deployment: detective.
• Config detective controls: after the fact.

Key takeaway: block noncompliant resources before creation → proactive controls.
Q002071:
Why this is correct:
Organization conformance packs deployed from the delegated administrator push the same rules and remediations to every account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual per account: toil.
• Trusted Advisor: not Config rules.
• Access Analyzer validation: policies.

Key takeaway: org-wide Config deployment → conformance packs.
Q002072:
Why this is correct:
Macie automated sensitive data discovery with an org delegated admin continuously samples buckets across all accounts at controlled cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily one-time jobs on every bucket: very expensive.
• GuardDuty S3 Protection: threats, not content.
• Inventory file names: unreliable.

Key takeaway: estate-wide sensitive data estimates → automated discovery.
